problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###  

**a. Verdict:**  
I have found a complete solution.  
The minimum number of rectangular tiles required is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Reduction to a permutation of uncovered squares.**  
   By permuting the columns we may assume that the unique uncovered square in each row and column is the diagonal cell \((i,i)\) for \(i=1,\dots ,2025\).

2. **Geometric restriction on a tile.**  
   A tile is an axis‑aligned rectangle, i.e. a product of a *consecutive* set of rows and a *consecutive* set of columns.  
   Because a rectangle may not contain any diagonal cell, every rectangle lies **entirely** either strictly **above** the main diagonal (all its rows are numbered smaller than all its columns) or strictly **below** it (all its rows are larger than all its columns).

3. **Lower bound – the “adjacent diagonal” cells.**  
   Consider the \(2024\) cells just above the diagonal,
   \[
   (1,2),\;(2,3),\dots ,\;(2024,2025).
   \]
   Two different such cells cannot belong to the same rectangle: if a rectangle contained both \((i,i+1)\) and \((i+1,i+2)\) then its row interval would contain \(i,i+1\) and its column interval would contain \(i+1,i+2\); consequently the rectangle would also contain the diagonal cell \((i+1,i+1)\), which is forbidden.  
   Hence each of the \(2024\) cells above the diagonal needs its **own** rectangle.  
   The same argument applied to the \(2024\) cells just below the diagonal,
   \[
   (2,1),\;(3,2),\dots ,\;(2025,2024),
   \]
   shows that they also require pairwise distinct rectangles.  
   Therefore any admissible tiling needs at least  

   \[
   2\,(2025-1)=4048
   \]

   rectangles.

4. **Construction attaining the bound.**  
   For every \(k=1,\dots ,2024\) place the two rectangles  

   \[
   \begin{aligned}
   R_k^{+}&=\{\text{rows }k\}\times\{\text{columns }k+1,k+2,\dots ,2025\},\\[2mm]
   R_k^{-}&=\{\text{rows }k+1,k+2,\dots ,2025\}\times\{\text{column }k\}.
   \end{aligned}
   \]

   * Each \(R_k^{+}\) lies completely above the diagonal because its single row index \(k\) is smaller than every column index in its column interval.  
   * Each \(R_k^{-}\) lies completely below the diagonal because every row index in its row interval exceeds the column index \(k\).  
   * The rectangles are pairwise disjoint: any square belongs either to a unique “above‑diagonal’’ rectangle or to a unique “below‑diagonal’’ rectangle, never to both.  

   The family \(\{R_k^{+},R_k^{-}\mid 1\le k\le2024\}\) consists of exactly \(4048\) rectangles and covers **all** off‑diagonal squares, leaving precisely the diagonal squares uncovered.  

5. **Conclusion.**  
   The lower‑bound argument shows that fewer than \(4048\) rectangles are impossible, and the explicit construction shows that \(4048\) rectangles are sufficient. Hence the minimum possible number of tiles is \(\boxed{4048}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**### Detailed Solution ###**  

Let \(n=2025\).  
The unit squares of the grid are indexed by ordered pairs \((i,j)\) with  
\(1\le i,j\le n\).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1.   Position of the uncovered squares  

Matilda must leave exactly one uncovered square in each row and each column.  
Consequently the set of uncovered squares forms a permutation matrix: after a suitable permutation of the columns there is a bijection \(\sigma\) such that the uncovered squares are  

\[
U=\{(i,\sigma(i))\mid 1\le i\le n\}.
\]

Renaming the columns by the permutation \(\sigma^{-1}\) we may (and shall) assume  

\[
U=\{(i,i)\mid 1\le i\le n\},
\tag{1}
\]

i.e. the main diagonal is uncovered and every other unit square must be covered.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.   Geometry of a permissible rectangle  

A rectangular tile is determined by two intervals of indices:

\[
\text{rows }[a,b]=\{a,a+1,\dots ,b\},\qquad
\text{columns }[c,d]=\{c,c+1,\dots ,d\},
\]

with \(1\le a\le b\le n,\;1\le c\le d\le n\).  
The tile covers exactly the squares  

\[
\{(i,j)\mid a\le i\le b,\;c\le j\le d\}.
\tag{2}
\]

Because of (1) the tile may not contain any diagonal cell \((t,t)\).  
If the row interval and the column interval intersect, i.e. if there exists an integer
\(t\) with \(a\le t\le b\) and \(c\le t\le d\), then the diagonal cell \((t,t)\) would belong to the tile, which is forbidden.  
Hence a permissible rectangle must satisfy either  

\[
b<c\qquad\text{(the rectangle lies **above** the diagonal)},
\tag{3a}
\]

or  

\[
d<a\qquad\text{(the rectangle lies **below** the diagonal)}.
\tag{3b}
\]

Thus every tile is wholly contained either in the strict upper‑triangular region
\(\{(i,j)\mid i<j\}\) or in the strict lower‑triangular region
\(\{(i,j)\mid i>j\}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.   A lower bound  

Consider the \(n-1\) squares that are **immediately** above the diagonal:

\[
U^{+}=\{(1,2),(2,3),\dots ,(n-1,n)\}.
\tag{4}
\]

Suppose two distinct squares \((i,i+1)\) and \((i+1,i+2)\) of \(U^{+}\) belonged to the same rectangle.
Because the rectangle is above the diagonal, its row interval must contain both rows
\(i\) and \(i+1\); its column interval must contain both columns \(i+1\) and \(i+2\).
Consequently the rectangle would also contain the diagonal cell \((i+1,i+1)\), contradicting (1).  
Hence **no rectangle can contain two different squares of \(U^{+}\)**.  
Therefore at least \(|U^{+}|=n-1\) distinct rectangles are required to cover the upper‑triangular part of the board.

Exactly the same argument applied to the \(n-1\) squares immediately below the diagonal,

\[
U^{-}=\{(2,1),(3,2),\dots ,(n,n-1)\},
\tag{5}
\]

shows that they also need pairwise distinct rectangles.  
Consequently any admissible tiling needs at least  

\[
(n-1)+(n-1)=2(n-1)
\tag{6}
\]

rectangles.

For \(n=2025\) this gives the numerical lower bound  

\[
2(2025-1)=4048.
\tag{7}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.   A tiling with \(2(n-1)\) rectangles  

Define, for each \(k\in\{1,2,\dots ,n-1\}\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
R_k^{+}&=\{\,\text{row }k\,\}\times\{\,\text{columns }k+1,k+2,\dots ,n\,\},\\[2mm]
R_k^{-}&=\{\,\text{rows }k+1,k+2,\dots ,n\,\}\times\{\,\text{column }k\,\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]

* **\(R_k^{+}\) lies above the diagonal.**  
  Its only row index is \(k\), while every column index in its column interval is \(\ge k+1\); thus condition (3a) holds.

* **\(R_k^{-}\) lies below the diagonal.**  
  Every row index in its row interval is \(\ge k+1\) whereas the column index is \(k\); thus condition (3b) holds.

* **Disjointness.**  
  The sets of squares covered by distinct rectangles are disjoint because the row (or column) intervals are disjoint: a square with column index \(>k\) can belong only to some \(R_k^{+}\); a square with row index \(>k\) and column index \(k\) can belong only to \(R_k^{-}\).

* **Coverage of the off‑diagonal cells.**  
  Let \((i,j)\) be a square with \(i\neq j\).

  *If \(i<j\)* (upper triangle): choose \(k=i\).  
  Then \(i\) is the unique row of \(R_i^{+}\) and \(j\ge i+1\) belongs to its column interval, so \((i,j)\in R_i^{+}\).

  *If \(i>j\)* (lower triangle): choose \(k=j\).  
  Then \(j\) is the unique column of \(R_j^{-}\) and \(i\ge j+1\) belongs to its row interval, so \((i,j)\in R_j^{-}\).

  Hence every off‑diagonal square belongs to exactly one rectangle of the family (8).

* **Uncovered squares.**  
  No rectangle contains a diagonal cell \((t,t)\) because for any \(k\) we have either \(t=k\) (then the column index of \(R_k^{+}\) is \(>k\)) or \(t=k\) (then the row index of \(R_k^{-}\) is \(>k\)). Thus the diagonal squares (1) remain uncovered.

The family (8) therefore yields a tiling consisting of exactly \(2(n-1)\) rectangles that satisfies all the required conditions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.   Minimality  

The lower bound (6) shows that no tiling can use fewer than \(2(n-1)\) rectangles, while the explicit construction provides a tiling that uses exactly \(2(n-1)\) rectangles. Consequently the minimum possible number of tiles is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]
